Operator:  
Good morning, and welcome to the Voltara Motors Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, please press star then two. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.  

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.  

Sarah Thompson:  
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Voltara Motors' Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Alex Rivera, CEO; John Ramirez, CFO; and other members of our leadership team.  

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.  

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.  

Alex Rivera:  
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q3 was a pivotal quarter for Voltara Motors. We made significant strides in key areas, including overcoming supply chain constraints through proactive mitigation strategies that have stabilized our production ramp, expanding our charging network with record utilization rates that are driving ancillary revenue growth, sustaining resilient average selling price trends across our model lineup and regions despite competitive pressures, and aggressively driving down battery costs per kWh to enhance our margin profile. We are particularly excited about the upcoming launch of the Voltara Aurora sedan and its anticipated acceleration of our market share in the premium EV segment with its 400-mile range and advanced 800V architecture.  

Now, I'll turn the call over to John Ramirez to discuss our financial performance in more detail.  

John Ramirez:  
Thank you, Alex. Good morning, everyone. For Q3, our revenue was $2.8 billion, representing a 32% increase year-over-year. Our gross margin was 28.5%, reflecting the benefits of our cost discipline and vertical integration. Operating expenses were $750 million, scaling efficiently with volume growth. Net income was $220 million. We are maintaining a strong balance sheet with $4.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents. Our guidance for next quarter is revenue of $3.2 to $3.4 billion, with gross margins expanding toward 30%.  

I'd now like to provide a detailed update on our supply chain constraints and the robust mitigation strategies we've implemented to safeguard our operations and deliver on our growth trajectory here at Voltara Motors. As you know, the automotive and EV sector continues to grapple with a perfect storm of disruptions—ranging from semiconductor scarcity and battery raw material volatility to geopolitical tensions and logistics bottlenecks. But I'm pleased to report that through proactive measures, we've limited the impact to our Q3 results and are positioning ourselves for outsized gains in the second half of the year and beyond.  

Let me start with the headwinds. Globally, semiconductor lead times for automotive-grade chips remain elevated at 28-32 weeks, per the latest SIA data, compared to a pre-pandemic norm of 12 weeks. This has directly constrained our production of high-volume models like the Voltara Spark sedan and Surge SUV. In Q3, chip shortages resulted in a 12% shortfall against our planned vehicle output, equating to approximately 18,000 units or $450 million in deferred revenue at our blended ASP of $25,000 per vehicle. On the battery front, lithium carbonate prices spiked 25% YoY to $18,000 per metric ton in Q3, driven by supply tightness in Australia and Chile amid weather disruptions and rising EV demand. This fed through to an 8% increase in our COGS for battery packs, pressuring gross margins by 120 basis points to 28.5%. Nickel and cobalt, key for our NMC 811 cathodes, saw similar volatility, with LME nickel futures up 15% intra-quarter due to Indonesian export curbs.  

Regionally, the picture varies. In North America, where 55% of our production is based out of our Gigafactory in Nevada and new Reno line, IRA-compliant sourcing has been a double-edged sword—boosting incentives but exposing us to U.S.-China trade frictions. Our U.S. cell production hit 95% capacity utilization, but imported modules from Asia faced 25% tariffs and Red Sea rerouting, adding $150 per kWh to landed costs. In Europe, comprising 30% of our volumes via our Berlin plant, EU Critical Raw Materials Act compliance has accelerated localization, but graphite anode supply from China—still 80% of global capacity—remains a pinch point, contributing to a 10% YoY rise in pack assembly times. Asia-Pacific, our 15% footprint in Thailand, benefited from lower logistics costs but suffered from Thailand floods delaying local PCB fabrication.  

Now, turning to our mitigation strategies—these are multi-layered, data-driven, and yielding tangible results. First, supplier diversification and dual-sourcing: We've reduced reliance on any single chip vendor from 40%—TSMC/Taiwan—to under 25%, locking in multi-year offtake agreements with Infineon, NXP, and emerging U.S. player GlobalFoundries. This secured 2.5 million units of ECUs and power modules through 2025, at a blended 10% discount to spot pricing. Early results? Q4 chip deliveries are tracking 20% ahead of Q3, enabling us to recoup 80% of that 18,000-unit shortfall.  

Second, battery ecosystem verticalization: We're accelerating our in-house cell production, ramping our 4680-style cylindrical cells—similar to Tesla's architecture but optimized for our 800V platform—to 50 GWh annual capacity by year-end, up from 20 GWh today. This represents 35% of our total 140 GWh needs, slashing external dependency. We've also hedged 70% of our 2024 lithium exposure via fixed-price contracts with Albemarle and SQM at $14,500/ton, and shifted 40% of our packs to LFP chemistry from CATL and BYD, which dropped cell-to-module costs by 15% to $85/kWh while qualifying for full IRA credits. Strategic partnerships shine here: Our JV with LG Energy Solution in Ohio is hitting 30 GWh run-rate, delivering 98% PPM defect rates, and we've inked a 100 GWh deal with Panasonic for U.S.-made prismatic cells starting Q4.  

Third, advanced tech and analytics: We've deployed AI-driven demand sensing via SAP IBP and our proprietary EV-specific forecasting model, integrating real-time data from 500+ suppliers. This has cut inventory turns from 8x to 12x annually, reducing working capital tied up in batteries from $1.2B to $900M—a 25% improvement—while minimizing stockouts to under 2%. On logistics, we're nearshoring 60% of Tier 2 components to Mexico under USMCA, bypassing Red Sea risks and trimming ocean freight costs by 18% via dedicated rail from maquiladoras.  

Fourth, regional resilience playbook: In Europe, we're collaborating with Northvolt on a sodium-ion pilot for low-end models, targeting 10% cost savings and cobalt-free chemistry by 2026. Stateside, IRA Section 45X credits are flowing at $40/kWh for our domestic packs, adding $200M to EBITDA this year. And in APAC, local content via our Thai JV with Foxconn exceeds 70%, shielding us from U.S. tariffs on exports.  

Strategically, these moves aren't just defensive—they're transformative. Our supply chain resilience score, per our internal Deloitte-audited framework, jumped from 72/100 in Q1 2023 to 88/100 today, outpacing peers like Rivian at 79 and legacy OEMs in the mid-70s. This positions us to capture market share as demand surges: Global EV sales are forecasted at 17 million units in 2024 per IEA, with U.S. penetration hitting 12%. We've already seen order backlog grow 22% QoQ to 150,000 units, with delivery-weighted ASP up 5% to $28,500 on premium trims.  

Looking forward, we expect supply constraints to ease materially: Chip lead times to 20 weeks by year-end, lithium stabilizing at $15,000/ton, and our mitigations delivering 300bps gross margin expansion to 31.5% in H2. Risks remain—e.g., potential U.S. election policy shifts or Congo cobalt unrest—but our $2.5B strategic inventory buffer and $1B undrawn credit facility provide ample dry powder.  

In summary, while supply chain pressures shaved 50bps off our full-year EPS guidance to $3.85-$4.05, our execution has contained the damage to low-single digits on EBIT and sets us up for 25%+ production growth in 2025.  

As we continue to scale our integrated EV ecosystem, let me dive deep into our charging network expansion and utilization rates, which remain a cornerstone of our vertical integration strategy. Our proprietary Voltara Charge Network—now the third-largest public DC fast-charging network globally—delivered record performance this quarter, underscoring the profitability of our 'charge-to-own' model. Let me walk you through the key metrics, trends, and strategic initiatives.  

First, on expansion. We deployed a net 7,200 new charging stalls across our network in Q3, bringing our global total to 52,400 stalls as of quarter-end. This represents a 28% sequential increase and puts us on track for our full-year guidance of 65,000 stalls by December 31st. Breaking it down regionally:  

In North America, which accounts for 55% of our network, we added 4,100 stalls, including 850 ultra-fast 350kW V3.5 units co-located with our retail showrooms and service centers. Adoption of the North American Charging Standard (NACS)—thanks to our early partnership with Tesla's Supercharger ecosystem—has accelerated this growth. We've now retrofitted 2,300 legacy CCS1 stalls to NACS, enabling seamless access for over 80% of the U.S. EV market, including Tesla, Ford F-150 Lightning, and Rivian R1T owners. This has boosted our U.S. stall count to 28,800, with a capex investment of $320 million this quarter, partially offset by $85 million in IRA transfer credits for domestic manufacturing.  

In Europe, we expanded by 1,900 stalls to reach 14,200 total, focusing on high-traffic corridors along the TEN-T network. Key wins include 450 MW-class chargers at IONITY hubs and our first bidirectional V2G pilots in Germany and the Netherlands, compatible with the upcoming EU Alternate Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) mandates. Utilization here is ramping fastest due to fleet electrification—think Uber's 10,000-vehicle commitment in the UK.  

China saw 1,200 new stalls, totaling 7,600, with emphasis on our 800V architecture chargers optimized for BYD and NIO partnerships. Amid the price wars, we're prioritizing high-density urban 'megahubs' in Shanghai and Shenzhen, each supporting 100+ stalls with liquid-cooled cables for 600kW peak rates. Emerging markets like India and Southeast Asia contributed 200 stalls, our first foothold via joint ventures with Tata Motors and Grab, targeting two-wheeler and light commercial EV fleets.  

This expansion was funded through a disciplined $1.2 billion capex allocation for the network YTD, with a 2.5x ROI projected within 24 months based on discounted cash flow models factoring 15% annual utilization growth.  

Now, turning to utilization rates, which are the real profitability driver. Our network-wide average utilization hit 48% in Q3—up 12 percentage points year-over-year and 5 points sequentially from Q2. This translates to 1.2 million charging sessions and 450 GWh of throughput, generating $185 million in charging revenue—a 62% YoY increase and now 18% of our total automotive segment EBITDA.  

Key trends and drivers: Peak-hour utilization reached 72% in urban corridors, with average dwell times dropping to 22 minutes thanks to our AI-optimized load balancing and dynamic pricing algorithms. Non-peak utilization improved to 32%, aided by B2B roaming agreements with Electrify America, ChargePoint, and EVgo, which now cover 95% of public U.S. chargers. Throughput per stall surged 35% YoY to 8.6 MWh, driven by our shift to higher-power units: 65% of new deployments are 250kW+, handling the energy demands of our Voltara Surge SUV (800V, 10-minute 10-80% charge) and fleet customers like Amazon's Rivian EDVs. Challenges persist in rural areas, where utilization lags at 28%, but we're addressing this with solar-plus-storage microgrids at 15% of sites, reducing grid dependency and qualifying for U.S. DOE grants.  

Strategically, we're monetizing beyond kWh sales. Ancillary revenue from software—route optimization via our Voltara App, now with 4.2 million MAUs—added $42 million, while premium subscriptions for unlimited 350kW access grew 40% to 750,000 users. Our V4 architecture rollout, with Magic Dock dual-port tech, positions us for CCS2/NACS convergence in Europe and the U.S. Looking forward, we guide Q4 utilization to 52-55%, with network revenue growing 70% YoY. Risks include supply chain delays on GB/T and CHAdeMO components in Asia, but hedges and our Nevada gigafactory mitigate this. Long-term, as EV adoption hits 25% U.S. market share by 2026 per BloombergNEF, we see network EBITDA margins expanding to 45% by 2027, rivaling Tesla's Supercharger economics.  

Before we open the floor to questions, I'd like to dive deeper into our Average Selling Price, or ASP, trends by model and region, as this has been a focal point given the dynamic EV market landscape. Our team has been laser-focused on balancing volume growth with margin discipline amid intensifying competition from players like Tesla, BYD, and legacy OEMs such as Ford and GM ramping up their Mustang Mach-E and F-150 Lightning lineups.  

Overall, our global blended ASP came in at $54,200 in Q3, marking a 4% increase year-over-year from $52,100 in Q3 2023, and a modest 2% sequential uptick from $53,100 in Q2 2024. This resilience is driven by a favorable product mix shift toward our higher-margin Surge SUV and Titan pickup platforms, which now represent 68% of total deliveries—up from 62% a year ago—coupled with strong uptake on software-enabled options like our Voltara Autonomy Suite (VAS), our L2+ ADAS package with over-the-air (OTA) upgradability to unsupervised FSD by 2025. However, we did see some ASP pressure in lower-end trims due to IRA lease credits in North America and aggressive pricing in China, where BYD's Seagull and Qin Plus models continue to set the pace in the sub-$25,000 segment.  

Let me break this down by model first, then by region, with key drivers and forward-looking initiatives.  

ASP trends by model: The Voltara Spark compact sedan, our entry-level offering, posted a Q3 ASP of $36,800, down 6% YoY from $39,100, but flat sequentially. Deliveries grew 15% YoY to 28,000 units, fueled by fleet sales to rideshare partners like Uber. The decline reflects a 10% price adjustment in the quarter to counter Xiaomi's SU7 and Zeekr's 001 in the affordable sedan space, plus higher take rates on base trims amid softening consumer demand for sub-$40k EVs. Margins held steady at 18% gross thanks to our 4680 cell vertical integration, which shaved $1,200 per unit in battery costs QoQ via improved silicon anode doping.  

Our volume hero, the Voltara Surge mid-size SUV/crossover, achieved $56,500 ASP, up 5% YoY from $53,800 and 3% sequentially. This model accounted for 52% of Q3 deliveries—112,000 units, +22% YoY—benefiting from a richer option mix. VAS adoption hit 42%, up from 35% YoY, adding $4,200 average per vehicle, and our new 800V architecture enabling 10-80% charging in 18 minutes, which resonated in premium markets. We've also layered in structural packs with LFP chemistry for the base RWD trim, reducing COGS by 8% without sacrificing range—now EPA 320 miles.  

The Voltara Titan full-size electric pickup saw ASP soar to $88,400, a robust 12% YoY gain from $78,900 and 4% QoQ lift, on 18,000 deliveries—+35% YoY. Cybertruck-like demand dynamics here, with 65% of buyers opting for the Tri-Motor AWD and Tow Pak, adding $12k ASP, plus regulatory credit monetization yielding $3,500 per unit. Early wins from our Megapack-sourced V2G bidirectional charging have boosted appeal for fleet operators like Amazon. Excluding leases and incentives, our 'transaction price ASP'—a metric we're now tracking akin to Tesla's—stood at $57,800 globally, underscoring underlying pricing power.  

By region: North America, 45% of revenue, had a regional ASP of $64,300, up 7% YoY and 3% QoQ, driven by a premium mix—Titan 25% of NA volume—and $7,500 IRA point-of-sale rebates flowing through as effective price uplift for qualifying buyers. California and Texas led with Surge Long Range trims averaging $62k, though Midwest fleet deals tempered the entry-level Spark to $41k. Competition from Rivian's R1T/R1S kept us aggressive on promotions, but VAS bundles mitigated 2% of potential erosion.  

Europe, 28% of revenue, saw $51,200 ASP, flat YoY but down 1% sequentially from subsidy normalization post the EU's €4,000 Green Deal incentives tapering in Germany and France. Surge dominated at 60% mix, with ASP boosted by 15% take-rate on our Winter Pak—heated everything plus aero wheels—amid harsh Q3 weather. UK volumes grew 30% YoY on ZEV mandate compliance, but VW ID.4 price cuts capped upside. Our response is localizing LFP production at our Magdeburg Gigafactory to hit €45k cost parity by Q4.  

China, 20% of revenue, posted $32,400 ASP, down 8% YoY from intensified price wars—BYD slashed Qin L to RMB 99,800 (~$14k), forcing our Spark JV with CATL to match at RMB 189,000 (~$26k). Still, +40% delivery growth to 45,000 units via our Shanghai plant's 0.2s/km fast-swap stations. Titan entry remains aspirational at RMB 550k (~$76k), with early traction from tech firms. Rest of World—APAC/LatAm/MEA, 7%—had $48,700 ASP, up 10% YoY on Surge exports to Australia and Korea, where our 500kW DC charging compatibility shines.  

Looking ahead, we're targeting mid-single-digit ASP expansion in Q4 through three pillars: mix optimization—ramping Titan to 25% of volume via Texas Gigafactory output doubling to 50k/month; tech-led monetization—VAS subscription conversion at 75% post-1-year ownership, projecting $1.5B recurring revenue by 2025, Tesla-style; and cost architecture—Q4 battery pack costs down 12% to $85/kWh via dry electrode coating at our Nevada cell fab, enabling $2k ASP-neutral price leadership in China. Risks include further Tesla Model 2/Y cuts or EU tariff hikes on Chinese LFP imports, but our 85% North American content shields us under USMCA. We expect Q4 blended ASP of $55,000-$56,000, with full-year at $54,500.  

As we examine one of the most critical levers driving our profitability and scalability in the EV space—battery costs per kWh— we've made tremendous progress here, outpacing industry benchmarks while navigating a complex global supply chain. Let me break it down with the latest data, trends, and our strategic outlook.  

In Q3, our average battery pack cost landed at $92 per kWh, a 12% sequential reduction from Q2's $105/kWh and a robust 28% year-over-year decline from $128/kWh in Q3 2023. This puts us firmly ahead of the BloombergNEF global average of $112/kWh for 2024 pack-level costs, and we're closing in on Tesla's reported sub-$100/kWh for their 4680 cells in high-volume Cybertruck production. To give you granularity: High-nickel NMC packs, used in our premium Aurora sedan and Surge SUV lines, averaged $108/kWh, down 15% YoY, thanks to optimized cathode loading at 4.5 NMP/kg. LFP packs, powering our mass-market Spark crossover, hit $76/kWh, a 22% drop, leveraging cell-to-pack (CTP) architectures that eliminate 20-30% of traditional module overhead.  

These figures are fully loaded—including cells, BMS integration, cooling systems, and factory-level assembly—excluding vehicle-level pack installation. Our gigafactory utilization in Nevada now exceeds 85%, contributing a $5/kWh cost advantage through scale.  

The industry-wide trajectory remains steeply downward, with pack costs falling 19% YoY globally per BNEF's latest tracking, on track for $80/kWh by end-2025. We're riding three megatrends: Economies of scale and oversupply—global cell capacity hit 2.5 TWh in 2024, up 40% YoY, creating pricing pressure. CATL and BYD flooded the market with LFP cells at $55-65/kWh ex-factory, forcing premium suppliers like LGES and Panasonic to match with NMC at $75-85/kWh. We've locked in multi-year offtake agreements with CATL for 50 GWh annually at fixed escalators below inflation.  

Chemistry shifts: LFP adoption surged to 45% of our mix from 25% last year, delivering 30% better cost-per-kWh at the expense of 10-15% lower energy density. Meanwhile, our NMC 811 cells are transitioning to NMCA blends with aluminum cathodes, shaving 8-10% off costs without density loss. Manufacturing innovations: Dry electrode coating—now in pilot at our Reno Gigafactory 2—cuts solvent costs by 25% and boosts throughput 50%. Combined with tabless designs akin to Tesla's 4680, we're targeting 15% cell-level savings by Q4 2025. Silicon-dominant anodes (10% Si content) are in validation, promising 20% more capacity at parity cost.  

Geography is reshaping the landscape: China, the undisputed low-cost leader, with CATL's Shenxing LFP at $52/kWh and BYD's Blade cells under $50/kWh. However, U.S. tariffs—100% on LFP imports—and IRA localization rules cap our exposure to 30% of mix. North America: Our Nevada output mirrors U.S. averages of $105/kWh but benefits from $45/kWh IRA tax credits, netting effective $60/kWh. Partners like Ultium Cells (GM-LGES JV) are at $110/kWh, validating our edge. Europe: Higher at $120/kWh due to stringent REACH regs and labor costs, but falling 18% YoY post-BMW and VW's in-housing. Our Berlin joint venture with Northvolt targets sub-$90/kWh by 2026. Supply chain resilience is key—we've derisked 70% of our lithium via U.S./Australian offtake, e.g., Piedmont Lithium contracts, amid LME prices dropping 60% YTD to $12,500/tonne.  

Batteries now represent 22% of our BOM, down from 32% in 2022, directly fueling our auto gross margins expanding to 28.4% this quarter. We're not just cutting costs; we're engineering for TCO leadership—our 400-mile Aurora at $0.035/mile battery depreciation beats ICE rivals. Looking ahead: Q4 target $88/kWh average, with LFP at $72/kWh. 2025 outlook: $75/kWh enterprise-wide, assuming 25% volume growth to 800k units. Longer-term: Sub-$60/kWh by 2027 via solid-state pilots partnered with QuantumScape for 500 Wh/kg prototypes and BCM recycling recovering 95% materials, $10/kWh credit. We're investing $2B in vertical integration, including anode copper foil production to capture 5-7% margin uplift. Competitively, this positions us to price our Spark at $28k ASP while maintaining 25%+ margins—critical against BYD's Seagull onslaught and Ford's IRA-fueled push. Risks remain: nickel volatility and potential IRA clawbacks, but our hedging covers 80% exposure. Battery deflation is our margin accelerator, and we're laser-focused on sustaining 20%+ annual reductions. This underpins our FY25 EPS guidance of $4.85-$5.20.  

Now, I'll hand the call back to the operator for the Q&A session.  

Operator:  
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. To withdraw, star then two. Our first question comes from Mike Chen at Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.  

Analyst 1:  
Thanks, and congrats on a strong quarter. John, on the supply chain front, you mentioned recouping most of the chip shortfall in Q4—can you elaborate on how the dual-sourcing with Infineon and others is playing out in terms of cost and reliability, especially with ongoing geopolitical risks?  

John Ramirez:  
Thanks, Mike. Great question. Our dual-sourcing has been a game-changer, securing those 2.5 million units at a 10% discount has not only stabilized supply but also improved our cost structure amid spot market volatility. Reliability-wise, defect rates are down 15% across these vendors, and with GlobalFoundries ramping U.S. production, we're insulated from Taiwan risks. Geopolitically, we're monitoring closely, but the Mexico nearshoring adds another layer of protection. This should fully offset the shortfall by year-end.  

Operator:  
Thank you. Next question from Lisa Patel at Morgan Stanley.  

Analyst 2:  
Hi, team. Sarah, no—John, on charging utilization hitting 48%, that's impressive. How sustainable is the 52-55% Q4 guide, particularly with rural lags and any seasonal demand softness?  

John Ramirez:  
Hi Lisa, thanks. Sustainability comes from our AI load balancing and roaming partnerships, which have smoothed out non-peak hours. Rural utilization at 28% is improving with microgrids, and seasonally, holiday travel should boost corridors. We're confident in the guide, as throughput per stall continues to climb with higher-power deployments.  

Operator:  
Thank you. Our next question is from David Kim at JPMorgan.  

Analyst 3:  
Good morning. Alex, with ASP holding up at $54,200 blended, how are you thinking about mix shift to Titan in 2025, and any updates on VAS subscription attach rates?  

Alex Rivera:  
Morning, David. Titan ramping to 25% of volume is key, with Texas Gigafactory doubling output. VAS subscriptions are converting at 75% post-ownership year one, adding meaningful recurring revenue. This mix, plus cost downs, supports our pricing power even in competitive markets.  

Sarah Thompson:  
Thank you for your questions. We have time for one more.  

Operator:  
Our final question from Emma Rodriguez at Barclays.  

Analyst 4:  
Thanks. John, battery costs at $92/kWh—fantastic progress. With LFP mix at 45%, how does this impact range in premium models, and thoughts on solid-state timeline?  

John Ramirez:  
Emma, thanks. LFP is primarily for mass-market like Spark, preserving NMC for Aurora and Surge where density matters. Range trade-offs are minimal with CTP efficiencies. Solid-state pilots with QuantumScape are on track for 2027 sub-$60/kWh, with prototypes hitting 500 Wh/kg. This keeps us ahead on TCO.  

Operator:  
Thank you. I would now like to turn the call back to Alex Rivera for closing remarks.  

Alex Rivera:  
Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us today. We are confident that Voltara Motors is well-positioned for continued success in the rapidly evolving automotive landscape. We look forward to updating you on our progress next quarter.  

Sarah Thompson:  
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes the Voltara Motors Q3 2024 earnings call. You may now disconnect.
